items.prompt: Which receipt section carries the verbatim quotes and policy hash the decision ran under?
options: inputs — the full DecisionInput: quotes as anchored, scores as scored, the policy version hash, and the gate as armed
items.explanation: Inputs verbatim is the design rule: a summarised input is a paraphrase, and paraphrases are the enemy of arguability. (obj-16-a)

items.prompt: Why are REFUSAL receipts first-class — full artifacts with the claim and quote preserved — even though nothing was published?
options: Because the human reviewing the escalation needs the exact evidence, and the refusal is precisely the decision that must be arguable after the fact
items.explanation: 'Nothing was published' is the most-scrutinised decision class: an unauditable refusal is indistinguishable from a bug. (obj-16-a)

items.prompt: What does verify_chain() == true actually prove?
options: That the digest was sent on time
That the log is intact — every receipt is exactly what the system wrote, in order, since genesis: memory integrity, not decision quality (that's the gold set's job)
That the system is within budget
items.explanation: Chain = memory integrity; gold = decision quality; together they make an action arguable. The distinction is worth reciting under questioning. (obj-16-b)

items.prompt: Someone edits Saturday's receipt to hide a bad publish. What happens at the next verify_chain() run?
options: The edit propagates to the digest silently
The link-rehash fails at the tampered row; the check reports the broken link, and the digest names the gap — tampering is detected, not prevented
Nothing — the log is append-only so edits are impossible
The whole chain re-hashes to match
items.explanation: The chain is tamper-EVIDENT: the rewrite breaks the cryptographic link to the next row, and the integrity check turns the edit into a visible incident. (obj-16-b)
